sections.title: Setting up Spring Boot with Redis

blocks.text:
Most Java teams do not use a Redis client directly. They use Spring, which handles the client lifecycle, configuration, exception translation and integration with caching, messaging, sessions and repositories. This chapter builds the foundation: dependencies, configuration for each topology, the choice between Lettuce and Jedis, pooling, TLS and the object at the centre of it all, `RedisConnectionFactory`.

### The layers

blocks.text:
Reading the figure from the top: your services use `Spring Cache` annotations or a `StringRedisTemplate`; those use a `RedisConnectionFactory`; the factory is implemented by `LettuceConnectionFactory` or `JedisConnectionFactory`; the client library owns the sockets. Everything above the factory is client-independent, which is why you can usually switch between Lettuce and Jedis by changing a dependency and one property.

### Dependencies

With Spring Boot 4.1 and Spring Data Redis 4.1 you add one starter. It brings Spring Data Redis and Lettuce.

blocks.code:
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <!-- optional: connection pooling for Lettuce or Jedis -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId>
        <artifactId>commons-pool2</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
blocks.title: pom.xml (fragment)

blocks.text:
There is also a `spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive` starter for the reactive templates (covered later in this Part). Spring Data Redis 4 uses Jackson 3 for its JSON features, which lives in the `tools.jackson` package; the starter and Spring Boot's dependency management take care of the version.

### Properties

For the common case of one server, configuration is a few lines of YAML.

blocks.code:
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost
      port: 6379
      database: 0
      username: shopstream      # ACL user, optional
      password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:}
      timeout: 500ms            # command timeout
      connect-timeout: 2s
blocks.title: application.yml

blocks.text: The Spring Boot reference documents these core keys: `spring.data.redis.host`, `port`, `database`, `username`, `password`, `url`, `ssl.enabled` and `ssl.bundle`. If you set `url` (for example `redis://user:secret@localhost:6379`, or `rediss://` for TLS), the host, port, username and password properties are ignored.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Check the timeout properties for your Boot version. The Lettuce default is no command timeout (see the previous Part). Spring Boot exposes `spring.data.redis.timeout` and `spring.data.redis.connect-timeout`. Verify in the application-properties appendix of the Boot version you use that they exist as spelled and that your connection factory really applies them: write a test that points the application at a port with nothing behind it, or a paused container, and check how long a call blocks.
For other topologies, Boot offers dedicated property groups. These names are long-standing; confirm them in the properties appendix for your exact Boot version.

blocks.code:
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      sentinel:
        master: mymaster
        nodes:
          - sentinel-1:26379
          - sentinel-2:26379
          - sentinel-3:26379
        password: ${REDIS_PASSWORD:}      # password for the Redis nodes, if different, see docs
blocks.title: application-sentinel.yml

blocks.code:
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      cluster:
        nodes:
          - node-1:6379
          - node-2:6379
          - node-3:6379
  max-redirects: 3
lettuce:
  cluster:
    refresh:
      adaptive: true
      period: 30s
blocks.title: application-cluster.yml

blocks.text:
What to notice: for cluster you list a few seed nodes, not every node; the client discovers the rest. The `lettuce.cluster.refresh` group turns on topology refresh (adaptive triggers and a periodic refresh), the setting that makes a client notice failovers promptly. Without it, a cluster client may learn about topology changes only from `MOVED` redirects.

If properties are not expressive enough, Boot lets you define a bean of type `RedisStandaloneConfiguration`, `RedisSentinelConfiguration`, `RedisClusterConfiguration` or `RedisStaticMasterReplicaConfiguration` and uses it instead. The static master/replica configuration is for environments that report non-public addresses through `INFO` (the Spring documentation names AWS as an example) and does not support Pub/Sub, because messages are not propagated across the individual servers. Jedis does not support master/replica mode.

### Lettuce or Jedis, and pooling

Lettuce is the default. To use Jedis, exclude `io.lettuce:lettuce-core` from the starter, add `redis.clients:jedis`, and (if both are present) select it with `spring.data.redis.client-type: jedis`. Unless you have a specific reason, stay on Lettuce.

Pooling in Spring behaves differently from what many developers expect:

- With Lettuce, **all** ordinary non-blocking, non-transactional operations share **one** native connection by default (the `shareNativeConnection` setting of `LettuceConnectionFactory` is `true`). Pooling applies to blocking and transactional connections, or to everything if you set `shareNativeConnection` to `false`.
- Boot auto-configures a pooled connection factory only if `commons-pool2` is on the classpath. Pool size is set under `spring.data.redis.lettuce.pool.*` (or `jedis.pool.*`), with `max-active`, `max-idle`, `min-idle` and `max-wait`.
- With Jedis, a pool is the normal way of working.

blocks.code:
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      lettuce:
        pool:
          max-active: 16
          max-idle: 16
          min-idle: 2
          max-wait: 500ms
blocks.title: application.yml (pool fragment)

### Customizing the client

When you need a Lettuce option that has no property (for example a `ClientOptions` timeout setting), register a customizer bean. Boot applies all `LettuceClientConfigurationBuilderCustomizer` beans to the client configuration builder (and `JedisClientConfigurationBuilderCustomizer` for Jedis; `ClientResourcesBuilderCustomizer` customizes Lettuce's shared `ClientResources`).

If the import above does not resolve in your project, let your IDE find `LettuceClientConfigurationBuilderCustomizer` on the classpath. Behaviour, not the import line, is what to rely on.

### TLS with SSL bundles

Spring Boot's SSL bundles describe key and trust material once and let components refer to them by name. For Redis you enable SSL and name the bundle:

blocks.code:
spring:
  ssl:
    bundle:
      pem:
        redis:
          truststore:
            certificate: file:/etc/secrets/redis-ca.pem
  data:
    redis:
      host: redis.internal
      port: 6380
      ssl:
        enabled: true
        bundle: redis
blocks.title: application-prod.yml

blocks.text:
The bundle key (`pem`, with a bundle named `redis`) follows Spring Boot's SSL bundle model; for mutual TLS, add a `keystore` with certificate and private key. Server-side TLS configuration is covered in the Operations and Security Part.

### The RedisConnectionFactory

`RedisConnectionFactory` is the abstraction every Spring Data Redis component receives: it hands out `RedisConnection` objects and translates client exceptions to Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy. In an ordinary Boot application you never create one by hand; you let Boot create it and inject it only where required (for example to build a custom `RedisTemplate` or a message listener container). Use `LettuceConnectionFactory#getConnection` only in infrastructure code, and always close what you get.

A quick way to prove the setup works is a startup check:

blocks.title: RedisStartupCheck.java
Key points
blocks.text:
- Add `spring-boot-starter-data-redis`; Lettuce is the default client and Jedis is optional.
- Core properties live under `spring.data.redis.*`; `url` overrides host, port, username and password.
- Use property groups or configuration beans for Sentinel, Cluster and static master/replica setups; enable cluster topology refresh.
- By default Lettuce shares one native connection; pooling needs `commons-pool2` and matters for blocking commands and transactions.
- Set timeouts explicitly and customize the client through customizer beans; use SSL bundles for TLS.

`RedisTemplate` is Spring's high-level Redis API. It does three jobs: it borrows and releases connections, it serializes your Java keys and values to bytes and back, and it groups the commands by data type into small interfaces. Learn its shape once and you can drive any data structure.

### Which template do I get?

Boot auto-configures two beans:

- `StringRedisTemplate`: keys and values are Strings, using string serializers. It is what you want for counters, flags, IDs, JSON that you serialize yourself, and anything you also want to read in `redis-cli`.
- `RedisTemplate<Object, Object>` (bean name `redisTemplate`): keys and values use **JDK serialization** by default.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: The default serializer is Java serialization. A `RedisTemplate` you create without configuration stores values with JDK serialization. The values are opaque binary, `redis-cli` shows `"\xac\xed\x00\x05..."`, other languages cannot read them, class changes break deserialization, and the Spring documentation warns that Java native serialization has been used for remote code execution through gadget classes. Always configure explicit serializers, or use `StringRedisTemplate`.

### The operations interfaces

The template does not have `get` or `hset` methods itself. You ask it for a typed view, and each view maps to one Redis data type:

rows: SET, GET, INCR, SET with NX or EX options
blocks.caption: Template views and the Redis types they drive.

blocks.text:
Each also has a *bound* variant (`boundValueOps(key)`, `boundHashOps(key)`, and so on) that fixes the key once, handy when you perform several operations on one key.

### A tour with ShopStream data

The next listing uses `StringRedisTemplate` for several of the ShopStream roles. Read it as a sampler: one method per structure.

blocks.title: ShopRedisOps.java

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `setIfAbsent(key, value, Duration)` is `SET key value NX PX ...` in one atomic command. Never write "check then set" as two calls.
- The `increment` methods are atomic server-side operations. `decrementStock` can go below zero; the flash-sale chapter in the Patterns Part shows how to guard against overselling with a script.
- `opsForHash()` is generic in its field and value types, so you declare `HashOperations<String, String, String>` to avoid casting.
- Return values like `Long` and `Boolean` can be `null` when the command is run inside a pipeline or transaction (the call is queued, not executed). Outside those modes they are non-null for these commands, but defensive handling costs little.
- Each call is a network round trip. For several commands in a row, use a pipeline (covered later in this Part) rather than looping.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Set TTLs when you write. `redis.expire(key, duration)` after `increment` is two commands. Between them the process can die and leave a key with no expiry. For strings, use `set(key, value, Duration)`. For hashes and other structures, run both in a script or transaction when the missing TTL would matter.

### Serializers

A `RedisSerializer<T>` has two methods: `serialize(T)` to bytes and `deserialize(byte[])` back. A template has four of them: for keys, values, hash keys and hash values (plus a default serializer used when a specific one is unset). The common rule is **String keys and hash keys, a JSON serializer for values**.

blocks.text:
#### Typed JSON values

For a cache of one type, the typed serializer is clean: no type information is written, and the JSON is exactly your object.

Product.java

blocks.text: Using it is then type-safe:

blocks.text:
In `redis-cli` the stored value is plain JSON, for example `{"id":"sku-1","name":"Kettle","price":24.90,"stock":120}`. Note that the template's bean name must not clash with Boot's `redisTemplate`; with two `RedisTemplate` beans, injection by generic type (as above) keeps them apart.

#### A generic JSON serializer

If one template must hold several types, use `GenericJacksonJsonRedisSerializer`. Without default typing, JSON objects deserialize into maps, not into your classes. Spring Data Redis 4's change notes are explicit: unlike its Jackson 2 predecessor, the new serializer does not enable default typing, and you opt in through its builder (`GenericJacksonJsonRedisSerializer.builder().enableDefaultTyping(...)`, with a type validator you choose).

blocks.title: GenericSerializerConfig.java

blocks.text:
The hard part of polymorphic JSON is security. Default typing writes class names into the data and instantiates classes named in the data when reading it; accepting any class name is dangerous. If you enable it, restrict it with a type validator to your own packages. Often the better design is not to need it: one typed serializer per cache, or store a "type" field yourself.

#### Migrating from Jackson 2

Applications moving to Spring Data Redis 4 will find the Jackson 2 serializers deprecated for removal: `GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer` becomes `GenericJacksonJsonRedisSerializer`, `Jackson2JsonRedisSerializer` becomes `JacksonJsonRedisSerializer`, and `Jackson2HashMapper` becomes `JacksonHashMapper`. The migration guide warns that Jackson 3 output can differ from Jackson 2 output (and `RedisSerializer.json()` now returns the Jackson 3 serializer), so values written by an old deployment may not be read the same way by a new one. Options: keep the Jackson 2 serializer temporarily so existing entries still deserialize, then migrate by letting entries expire, or write a one-off migration job. For caches the simplest strategy is often to change the key prefix (for example add a version, `product:v2:`), so old and new entries never collide.

### Key design in the template layer

Do not build keys by scattering string concatenations around the code. Put key construction in one small class per domain:

blocks.title: Keys.java

blocks.text:
Central key builders make renames, prefixes per environment and versioned keys (`v2:`) trivial, and let you grep for every use of a key.

### Exceptions

Spring translates driver exceptions into its `DataAccessException` hierarchy: `RedisConnectionFailureException` when the connection fails, `QueryTimeoutException` on command timeouts, `RedisSystemException` for others. Catch these (or `DataAccessException`) at the boundary where you decide how to degrade (see the chapter on connection management in the Java clients Part).

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why does my RedisTemplate show strange keys like "\\xac\\xed\\x00\\x05t\\x00..." in redis-cli? Because a plain `RedisTemplate` serializes keys with Java's JDK serialization. Use `StringRedisTemplate`, or set `StringRedisSerializer` as key and hash-key serializer and a JSON serializer for values. The same mismatch explains "I wrote with one template and cannot read with another" bugs: two templates with different serializers see different bytes.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- `StringRedisTemplate` for strings; `RedisTemplate` needs explicit serializers because its default is JDK serialization.
- Use `opsForValue`, `opsForHash`, `opsForList`, `opsForSet`, `opsForZSet`, `opsForStream`; bound variants fix the key once.
- Keys and hash keys: `StringRedisSerializer`. Values: `JacksonJsonRedisSerializer<T>` for one type, `GenericJacksonJsonRedisSerializer` with care for mixed types.
- Spring Data Redis 4 uses Jackson 3; the Jackson 2 serializers are deprecated for removal and the byte output can differ.
- Centralize key names and handle `DataAccessException` where you decide the degradation policy.

A Redis hash is a natural home for a flat object: field names are property names, field values are property values, and you can read or change one property without touching the others. The question is how a Java object becomes a hash and back. Spring Data Redis answers it at two levels. **Hash mappers** convert an object to a `Map` that you store yourself with `HashOperations`. **Redis repositories** go further: you annotate a class, extend `CrudRepository`, and Spring writes the hash, the indexes and the expiry for you. This chapter shows both, and is candid about when the second is the wrong tool.

### Hash mappers

The `HashMapper` interface has two methods: `toHash(object)` and `fromHash(map)`. Spring Data Redis ships several implementations:

rows: Spring Data's object-to-hash mapping (the engine behind Redis repositories)
Can flatten nested structures; successor to `Jackson2HashMapper`
blocks.caption: Hash mapper implementations.

blocks.text: The reference documentation shows the pattern with `ObjectHashMapper`, using binary hash fields and values:

blocks.title: HashMapping.java

blocks.text: For hashes that humans and other tools should read, you want String fields and values. `JacksonHashMapper` produces a `Map<String, Object>`, and `DecoratingStringHashMapper` converts the values to strings so you can use a `StringRedisTemplate`:

blocks.title: JacksonHashDemo.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: after `save`, `HGETALL product:sku-1` shows readable fields (`id`, `name`, `price`, `stock`). With `flatten()`, nested objects become dotted fields (`address.city`); without it, nested objects are stored as embedded JSON strings. The documentation warns that flattening cannot cope with property names or map keys that contain dots or brackets, and that a flattened hash cannot always be mapped back to an object. If you used `Jackson2HashMapper` before, the migration notes describe a `jackson2CompatibilityMode()` option on the builder to keep the old representation readable; choose `flatten()` or `hierarchical()` to match whatever your old data used.

The advantage of storing a product as a hash rather than a JSON string is partial access: `HINCRBY product:sku-1` `stock -1` changes the stock without reading or rewriting the rest. The cost is that nested data is awkward and every field is a string. If you mostly read or write the whole object, a JSON string value is simpler (see the previous chapter).

### Redis repositories

A Redis repository stores an annotated Java object as a hash and maintains extra structures for lookups. You get a familiar Spring Data interface; you pay with several Redis commands per save and per query.

blocks.title: UserSession.java
UserSessionRepository.java

blocks.text:
The annotations in plain words:

- `@RedisHash("session")` marks the class as a Redis entity and names its **keyspace**, the prefix of its keys. Without a value, the fully qualified class name is the keyspace. The `timeToLive` attribute sets a default expiry in seconds.
- `@Id` marks the identifier. If it is a `String` and null on save, Spring generates a random UUID, as the reference documentation's examples show.
- `@Indexed` on a property maintains a secondary index so that you can query by it. Only indexed properties can be used in derived queries.
- `@TimeToLive` marks a numeric property (or method) that holds the entity's time to live. On read it holds the remaining TTL in seconds; `-1` means no expiry. Do not put `@TimeToLive` on both a property and a method of the same class.

Usage is plain Spring Data:

blocks.title: SessionService.java

blocks.text:
In a Boot application with Spring Data Redis on the classpath, repository support is auto-configured; the property `spring.data.redis.repositories.enabled` can turn it off. If your application also uses another Spring Data module (JPA, for instance), Spring Data may log that it entered strict repository configuration mode, where it decides which module owns a repository interface by looking at its domain class annotations. Annotating the entity with `@RedisHash` makes the assignment unambiguous. Use `@EnableRedisRepositories` when you need to set options such as the keyspace-events mode.

### What is actually stored

Redis repositories are easy to use and surprisingly busy. The reference documentation shows the commands issued on insert; for our session they correspond to the following (typical, trimmed output):

blocks.text: Four kinds of key appear:

rows: The entity: one field per property, plus `_class`
The IDs of all entities in the keyspace; backs `findAll`, `count`
A secondary index: the IDs whose property has this value
Names of the index sets this entity is in, so they can be cleaned up on update and delete
blocks.caption: Keys written by a Redis repository (keyspace "session").

blocks.text:
Geo-indexed properties (`@GeoIndexed`) use a Redis geo set instead of a plain set.

A save therefore performs: write the hash, add the ID to the keyspace set, add it to each index set, record the index names. An update replaces the hash and removes stale index entries first (`DEL`, `HMSET`-style write, `SMEMBERS` on the `:idx` set, then removals and re-adds). A finder like `findByUserId` does `SINTER` on the index sets, then one `HGETALL` for **each** matching ID. None of this is wrapped in a transaction by the documentation's description, so a crash in the middle can leave an index and a hash out of step.

### Expiry and phantom copies

When a repository entity has a TTL, Spring sets `EXPIRE` on the hash. But Redis cannot expire a single member of a set, so the ID would stay forever in the keyspace set and in the index sets after the hash vanishes. To clean up, Spring Data Redis subscribes to Redis **keyspace notifications** (expired-key events) and removes the dangling index entries when the event arrives. For that it needs the expired object's values, which are gone by then, so it keeps a **phantom copy**: a second copy of the entity that expires five minutes after the original (this is described in the reference documentation; the copy has a `:phantom` suffix in the implementation). The consequences:

- It enables a `RedisKeyExpiredEvent` that your code can listen for, containing a copy of the expired object.
- It doubles the storage for entities with a TTL. The `shadowCopy` setting (the reference documentation writes it as `shadowCopy = OFF`; look up where it is declared in your version) disables the copy, and the expired event then carries only the ID.
- The keyspace listener alters the server setting `notify-keyspace-events` if it is not already set. It does not override an existing value, so set it correctly yourself (the expired-events flag must be on). On managed services where `CONFIG` is blocked (the documentation names AWS ElastiCache) the listener fails, and you set `keyspaceNotificationsConfigParameter` to an empty string and configure the server through the provider's mechanism.
- By default the expiry listener is **not started** with the application. You can start it with the application or on the first insert of an entity with a TTL, through the `enableKeyspaceEvents` option of `@EnableRedisRepositories`.

blocks.title: RedisRepoConfig.java

blocks.text: Check the Javadoc of `EnableKeyspaceEvents` in your version for the available modes.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Pub/Sub is not durable, so index cleanup can be missed. The reference documentation states it plainly: repositories rely on Pub/Sub messages for residual index cleanup. If a key expires while the application is down (or disconnected), the event is lost and index sets may keep references to IDs whose hash no longer exists. Redis also cannot expire individual members of an index set. A query can then return fewer objects than the index suggests, and index sets grow. If this matters, do not use TTLs with indexed entities, or schedule your own cleanup.

### Limits and when not to use repositories

Redis has no query language over hashes, so every capability is built from the primitives above, and the costs show up:

- **Write amplification.** One save is several commands, more when indexes change. Compare with one `HSET`.
- **N+1 reads.** A finder loads each matching entity with its own `HGETALL`. A query returning 5,000 sessions is 5,000 reads plus the `SINTER`.
- **Query power.** Equality on indexed properties and simple combinations. No range queries or full text over repository indexes; for those use the Query Engine (see the search chapter of the Patterns Part).
- **Cluster.** The keys involved (entity hash, keyspace set, index sets) hash to different slots, and the multi-key reads and cleanup are hard to fit into a cluster. Check the reference documentation for your version before relying on repositories with Redis Cluster.
- **Big keyspace sets.** The keyspace set grows with the number of entities; `findAll` over millions of entities is a large read.
- **Format.** Data is stored in Spring Data's own hash format with a `_class` field; other services must follow it.

A decision guide:

rows: Cache entity by key, read whole object
JSON string via `RedisTemplate` or Spring Cache
Quick CRUD of small objects with a few lookup fields
Large result sets, ranges, text search, joins
A database, or Redis Query Engine
Redis repositories are not built for this

blocks.text: Why session storage is a good fit and a bad fit. Sessions are looked up by ID, expire on their own and are small, which suits a hash with a TTL. Looking up "all sessions of user u-42" through an index is the part that carries the cleanup problem above. Spring Session (covered later in this Part) is built for this job and is usually the better choice.

### LAB 7.1 · Inspect what a repository writes

1. Start a local Redis with `docker run -d --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:8` and a Spring Boot app with the `UserSession` entity and repository above.
2. Call `login("u-42", "10.0.0.7")` twice from a test or a `CommandLineRunner`.
3. In `redis-cli`, run `SCAN 0 MATCH session* COUNT 100` and note every key type you see. Use `TYPE`, `HGETALL`, `SMEMBERS` and `TTL` on each.
4. Call `findByUserId("u-42")` while running `redis-cli MONITOR` in another terminal (only on a development instance). Count the commands issued and compare with a hand-written `HGETALL` by ID.
5. Wait for the TTL to expire (use a short `timeToLive`, for example 20 seconds) and look again at the keyspace set and the index set. Which entries are still there? Try again with the expiry listener disabled.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why does saving an entity with a Redis repository issue more than one command, and what is the risk? The repository maintains a keyspace set and secondary index sets in addition to the entity hash, and updates must clean old index entries. These writes are not one atomic operation, and expiry cleanup depends on non-durable Pub/Sub keyspace events, so indexes can drift from the data. For simple key-based access use `RedisTemplate`/`HashOperations`; use repositories where convenience beats the overhead.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A `HashMapper` converts objects to hash maps; `ObjectHashMapper` is binary, `JacksonHashMapper` (Jackson 3) can flatten nested objects, and the Jackson 2 mapper is deprecated.
- Hashes allow partial updates (`HINCRBY`); JSON strings are simpler for whole-object access.
- `@RedisHash`, `@Id`, `@Indexed` and `@TimeToLive` define a repository entity; keys are the hash, a keyspace set, index sets and an `:idx` tracker.
- TTL cleanup relies on keyspace notifications and phantom copies, which are neither free nor durable.
- Expect write amplification and N+1 reads; avoid repositories for large result sets, complex queries and cluster-heavy designs.

Almost every Spring application eventually asks the same question: "I already computed this, why am I computing it again?" The Spring Cache abstraction answers it with annotations. You mark a method with `@Cacheable`, Spring wraps the bean in a proxy, and the proxy checks a cache before calling the method. Redis is one of the stores that can sit behind that cache. This chapter shows how the pieces fit, how to configure them for a production service such as ShopStream's catalog-service, and which mistakes cost the most time.

The caching patterns themselves (cache-aside, stampede protection, consistency with the database) are covered in the Patterns part. Here we focus on the Spring machinery: what is stored under which key, how long it lives, how it is serialized, and what the annotations do and do not guarantee.

### The abstraction in one picture

Spring Cache has two layers. The **annotations** (`@Cacheable`, `@CachePut`, `@CacheEvict`) describe intent on your methods. The **CacheManager** is a registry that hands out named `Cache` objects. When Redis is the backing store, the manager is a `RedisCacheManager` and each named cache is a `RedisCache` whose entries are plain Redis string keys.

blocks.code:
caller ─► proxy ─► CacheInterceptor ─► RedisCache ─► RedisCacheWriter ─► Lettuce ─► Redis
               │                                   │
               └── miss: call the real method ◄────┘   key = prefix + cacheName + "::" + key

blocks.text:
Because the mechanism is a proxy, the annotation only works when the call comes from another bean through the Spring-managed reference. We will return to that limitation in the pitfalls section.

### Minimal setup

Add `spring-boot-starter-cache` next to `spring-boot-starter-data-redis`, enable caching, and tell Boot to use Redis. With these three steps Boot builds a `RedisCacheManager` for you.

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

spring:
  cache:
    type: redis
    redis:
      time-to-live: 10m
      cache-null-values: false
      key-prefix: "shopstream:"
      use-key-prefix: true
      enable-statistics: true
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost

blocks.text: The `spring.cache.redis.*` properties set defaults for every cache that Boot creates: `time-to-live` is the entry TTL, `cache-null-values` decides whether a `null` result is stored, `key-prefix` and `use-key-prefix` control the prefix, and `enable-statistics` switches on hit and miss counting (used by the metrics section later). These properties are enough for a first version. When you need a different TTL per cache, a different serializer, or jitter, you define the `RedisCacheManager` yourself, which we do below.

blocks.text:
### The three annotations

Here is a catalog service that uses all three. The record `ProductDto` is the cached value.

blocks.title: ProductService.java

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `@Cacheable` looks first. On a hit it returns the cached value and the method body never runs. On a miss it runs the body and stores the result. The Redis key is `products::42` (cache name, two colons, the key).
- `@CachePut` always runs the method and always writes the result. Use it when the method already has the fresh value and you want the cache to hold it.
- `@CacheEvict` removes one entry, or every entry of the cache with `allEntries = true`. Eviction is usually safer than put after a write, because a stale put can overwrite a newer value in a race; the Patterns part discusses this trade-off.
- `unless` is evaluated after the method ran and can see `#result`. `condition` is evaluated before and decides whether caching applies at all.

### Keys and key generation

If you give no `key`, Spring uses its default key generator: no arguments gives a fixed internal key, one argument uses that argument, several arguments are combined into a `SimpleKey`. Redis then needs a string, so `RedisCache` converts the key with a conversion service. Simple types such as `Long` and `String` convert naturally. A custom object converts only if it has a useful `toString()`, otherwise you get an exception complaining that the key cannot be converted to a string.

The robust habit is to write the key explicitly with SpEL (`key = "#id"`, `key = "#userId + ':' + #locale"`). It also documents the Redis key you will see in `redis-cli`.

The default prefix is the cache name followed by `::`. You can change it in the configuration with `prefixCacheNameWith("shopstream:")` (a fixed prefix in front of the name) or `computePrefixWith(cacheName -> ...)` (a function). Prefixing matters when several services share one Redis: without a prefix, two services that both define a cache named `products` overwrite each other's entries.

### Your own RedisCacheManager: TTLs, serializers, jitter

The following configuration gives the `products` cache a 30 minute TTL with jitter, a short-lived `stock-view` cache of one minute, and JSON values instead of Java serialization.

blocks.title: RedisCacheConfig.java

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `entryTtl(Duration)` sets a fixed TTL. The overload that accepts a function (a `RedisCacheWriter.TtlFunction`) is called per entry with the key and value, and that is how the jitter is produced: every entry gets 30 minutes plus a random 0 to 299 seconds, so a batch of products cached together does not all expire in the same second (the avalanche problem described in the Patterns part).
- `disableCachingNullValues()` means a `null` result is not cached. If a `@Cacheable` method returns `null` and you did not add `unless = "#result == null"`, the put fails with an `IllegalArgumentException` that names the cache. Either choice is valid, but you must pick one on purpose.
- `BatchStrategies.scan(1000)` makes `allEntries = true` use `SCAN` instead of `KEYS`. The default batch strategy uses `KEYS`, which blocks a large keyspace; this is the one-line fix. With Jedis, `SCAN` is only supported for non-clustered setups.
- `serializeValuesWith` replaces the default value serializer. Out of the box `RedisCache` uses Java native serialization (`JdkSerializationRedisSerializer`), which needs `Serializable` classes, is opaque in `redis-cli`, and breaks when the class changes. JSON is readable and survives refactoring better.
- `enableStatistics()` on the builder turns on local hit and miss counters. It is the same switch as the `spring.cache.redis.enable-statistics` property.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: One serializer per cache, not one for all types. `JacksonJsonRedisSerializer<ProductDto>` knows exactly one target type. If you put it on the defaults, a cache holding a `List<String>` fails on read. Give typed serializers to individual caches as above, or use `GenericJacksonJsonRedisSerializer` for mixed content; remember that it does not write type information unless you enable default typing in its builder, and that default typing has security implications for untrusted data. The template chapter earlier in this Part explains the serializers in detail.

### sync = true, locking and the stampede

When a popular entry expires, many threads may miss at once and all call the database. `@Cacheable(sync = true)` tells Spring that only one thread per key may compute the value while others wait for it. The important detail is the scope: this is a lock **inside one JVM**. If catalog-service runs on ten instances, each instance may still compute the value once, so up to ten database calls can happen for one expiry. That is usually acceptable, and far better than hundreds. For cross-instance protection you need a Redis-based lock or single-flight, covered in the Patterns part.

Two further points. With `sync = true` you can use only one cache name, and the `unless` attribute is not supported together with it, so a `null` result must be handled another way. Separately, `RedisCacheWriter.lockingRedisCacheWriter(...)` is a different thing: it locks at the **cache** level (not the entry) with a lock key in Redis to make `putIfAbsent` and `clean` non-overlapping. It costs extra round trips and the reference documentation describes it as an opt-in; most applications leave the default lock-free writer in place.

### Pitfalls that bite in practice

#### Self-invocation

Calling a cached method from another method of the same class bypasses the proxy, so the annotation does nothing.

blocks.title: SelfInvocation.java

blocks.text:
The fix is to move the cached method into another bean and inject it, which is also the cleaner design.

#### Large and dynamic keys

A key such as `#filters` where `filters` is a big object produces a long string key per call, and almost every call is a miss. Keep keys short and deterministic, hash large inputs yourself, and avoid caching results of queries whose parameters are nearly unique (free text search).

#### Caching mutable or huge objects

A cache entry is serialized on put and deserialized on get, so mutating the returned object does not change the cache (unlike an in-memory map). The flip side: caching a 5 MB list of products makes each hit move 5 MB across the network. Cache the pieces you actually reuse and keep values small.

#### Transactions

By default a `@CachePut` writes to Redis immediately, even if the surrounding database transaction later rolls back. `RedisCacheManager.builder(...).transactionAware()` makes cache puts and evictions wait until the transaction commits. Even then, cache and database can disagree for a short time; see the consistency chapter in the Patterns part.

#### Failures of Redis

When Redis is down, a cached method throws, and the user sees an error although the database is healthy. Implement `CachingConfigurer` (or define a `CacheErrorHandler`) that logs and returns, so that a Redis outage degrades to "slower" rather than "broken". Test this path on purpose.

#### Reactive methods

Spring's cache abstraction can cache methods that return `Mono` or `Flux`; it needs a cache that supports asynchronous retrieval, which `RedisCache` does. We come back to this in the reactive chapter.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why did my @Cacheable method not cache anything? Most likely one of four causes: caching is not enabled (`@EnableCaching` is missing); the method is called from inside the same class so the proxy is bypassed; the method is not public or the class is final in a way that prevents proxying; or the result is `null` and null caching is disabled. A fifth cause is a key that is different on every call. Check with `redis-cli --scan --pattern 'shopstream:*'` to see what really gets stored.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- `@Cacheable`, `@CachePut` and `@CacheEvict` work through a proxy; calls from inside the same class are not cached.
- Redis keys look like `cacheName::key`; set the key explicitly with SpEL and use a prefix when services share a Redis.
- Define `RedisCacheManager` yourself for per-cache TTLs, jitter (a TTL function), JSON serializers and a `SCAN` batch strategy for `allEntries`.
- The default value serializer is Java serialization; prefer typed JSON serializers per cache.
- `sync = true` is a per-JVM lock, not a distributed one.
- Add a `CacheErrorHandler` so that a Redis outage does not turn into application errors.

Redis Pub/Sub lets one client publish a message to a channel and every currently subscribed client receive it. It is fire-and-forget: Redis keeps no copy, so a subscriber that is offline when the message is published never sees it. That makes it a good fit for transient signals (cache invalidation notices, "something changed" nudges, live updates to a dashboard) and a bad fit for work that must not be lost; for that, use Streams. The Pub/Sub concept itself is explained in the data structures part; this chapter shows how Spring wires it up.

### The pieces

rows: Owns the subscription connection and a thread pool; delivers messages to listeners
Interface with `onMessage(Message message, byte[] pattern)`; you implement it
Wraps a plain object and calls one of its methods, converting the payload for you
What to subscribe to: an exact channel, or a glob pattern such as `orders.*`
Publishes a message to a channel
blocks.caption: Spring Data Redis messaging types.

blocks.text:
Spring documents the container as the component that "is responsible for all threading of message reception". One connection and one thread are shared by all listeners, subscriptions are created lazily, and you can add or remove listeners while the application is running.

### Publishing

Publishing is one line on a template. Under the hood it runs the `PUBLISH` command; treat it as best effort, because nothing tells your code whether anyone was listening.

blocks.text:
### Subscribing with a container and a listener

Use this to keep the local in-memory cache of each catalog-service instance in sync: when one instance changes a product, every instance learns about it.

blocks.title: PubSubConfig.java
LocalCacheInvalidator.java

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `onMessage` receives raw bytes. If you published through a `StringRedisTemplate`, decode them as UTF-8.
- The second argument is the pattern that matched, or `null`/empty when the subscription was an exact channel. One listener can serve several topics.
- The container starts automatically with the application context (it is a `SmartLifecycle`) and stops on shutdown.

### Subscribing with MessageListenerAdapter

A `MessageListenerAdapter` lets any plain class become a listener, so your business code does not depend on Spring types. The adapter deserializes the payload with its configured serializer and calls the named method.

blocks.title: OrderNotifyConfig.java

blocks.text:
The adapter's default method name is `handleMessage`, and an exception in your method is caught and handled by the container (by default it is logged), so one bad message does not kill the subscription.

### Annotation-driven listeners

Spring Data Redis 4.x also has an annotation style, similar in spirit to Spring's JMS and Kafka listeners. A bean method is marked `@RedisListener`, and a configuration class carries `@EnableRedisListeners` next to a `RedisMessageListenerContainer` bean. The reference documentation shows the attribute as `topic`, with a plain string meaning a channel and a glob meaning a pattern.

blocks.title: AnnotatedListener.java

blocks.text:
The reference documentation says nothing about which version introduced it, and at least one blog post writes the attribute as `topics`. Check the Javadoc of the version you use before copying either spelling. The container-based style above works on every version, which is why this book uses it as the primary example.

### Reliability limits you must design around

A subscriber only receives messages published while it is connected and subscribed. Four consequences follow.

- **No history, no replay.** A restart, a network blip or a Sentinel failover creates a gap. Messages published in the gap are gone.
- **No acknowledgement and no retry.** Redis does not know whether your listener finished. If `onMessage` throws, the message is not redelivered.
- **No load balancing.** Every subscriber gets every message. Ten notification-service instances on one channel send ten emails. For "one worker handles each message", use a stream with a consumer group.
- **Slow subscribers are cut off.** Redis buffers outgoing messages per client; a subscriber that cannot keep up is disconnected once its output buffer exceeds the `client-output-buffer-limit pubsub` setting.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not use Pub/Sub for events that must not be lost. Payment confirmations, stock reservations and order state changes belong in a stream (or a database outbox). Use Pub/Sub for hints that can be recomputed: "product 42 changed, drop your local copy". If a missed hint is only a few seconds of staleness, Pub/Sub is the right size of tool.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Keep the listener fast. The container delivers messages on its own threads. A listener that calls a slow HTTP service blocks delivery of the following messages. Hand the work to a bounded executor of your own, and give the container a suitable `TaskExecutor` through `setTaskExecutor` in anything beyond a demo.

On a Redis Cluster, a classic `PUBLISH` is broadcast to every node, which is costly at volume. Sharded Pub/Sub (`SSUBSCRIBE`, `SPUBLISH`) keeps traffic within one shard; check the support of your Spring Data Redis and client version before relying on it.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between Redis Pub/Sub and Redis Streams? Pub/Sub delivers to the subscribers connected right now and keeps nothing; Streams append messages to a log that is stored, can be read later, and with consumer groups can be shared among workers with acknowledgement and redelivery. Choose Pub/Sub for ephemeral notifications, Streams when a message must be processed at least once.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- `RedisMessageListenerContainer` owns the subscription connection and threads; define it as a bean and register listeners with `ChannelTopic.of(...)` or `Topic.pattern(...)`.
- Implement `MessageListener` for raw bytes, or wrap a POJO with `MessageListenerAdapter`; `@RedisListener` with `@EnableRedisListeners` is the annotation style in Spring Data Redis 4.x.
- Publish with `StringRedisTemplate.convertAndSend(channel, message)`.
- Messages are not stored, acknowledged or load balanced. Anything critical goes to Streams.
- Keep listeners fast and give the container a sensible `TaskExecutor`.

A Redis Stream is an append-only log. Producers add entries with `XADD`; consumers read them either independently (`XREAD`) or as a team through a **consumer group** (`XREADGROUP`), where Redis hands each entry to exactly one consumer of the group and remembers it in a **pending entries list** (PEL) until the consumer acknowledges it with `XACK`. The stream data type, groups and the PEL are explained in the data structures part; here we put them to work in ShopStream: order-service appends order events to `stream:orders`, and notification-service, running as several instances in the consumer group `notifier`, sends the emails.

Spring Data Redis supports streams on three levels: `StreamOperations` (one command per method), `StreamMessageListenerContainer` (a polling loop that calls your listener), and the reactive `StreamReceiver` (shown in the next chapter).

### Producing events

`opsForStream()` returns the `StreamOperations`. With a `StringRedisTemplate` an entry is a map of strings.

blocks.title: OrderEventProducer.java

blocks.text:
`add` returns the generated ID such as `1760000000000-0`. The last argument of `trim` asks for **approximate** trimming (`MAXLEN ~`), which Redis can do cheaply in whole internal blocks; exact trimming is slower. An unbounded stream is a memory leak that grows slowly, so decide on a trimming policy on day one.

### Creating the group

A group must exist before consumers can read through it. Create it once at startup; if it already exists Redis answers with a `BUSYGROUP` error, which you treat as success.

blocks.title: StreamGroupInitializer.java
Gotcha
blocks.text: The group cannot be created on a stream that does not exist yet. The `createGroup` call of the template fails if `stream:orders` has never received an entry, because it does not use the `MKSTREAM` option of `XGROUP CREATE`. Either create the group after the first event is produced (seed the stream at deployment), or execute `XGROUP CREATE` `stream:orders notifier 0 MKSTREAM` from a migration script. `ReadOffset.from("0")` means the group starts with the oldest entry; `$` means only new entries.

### Consuming with StreamMessageListenerContainer

The container runs a polling loop on its own executor and calls your `StreamListener` for each entry. There are three decisions to take: which consumer name this instance uses, whether the container acknowledges automatically, and what happens on error.

blocks.title: StreamConsumerConfig.java
OrderEventListener.java

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `ReadOffset.lastConsumed()` translates to the `>` ID of `XREADGROUP`: "give me entries never delivered to anyone in this group". It does not return entries that are already pending for you after a crash; the recovery section deals with those.
- `autoAcknowledge(false)` means that the listener must call `acknowledge`. The shorter `container.receiveAutoAck(...)` variant acknowledges when the entry is **delivered** to the listener, before your code succeeds. An exception then loses the entry, which is "at most once". For orders, we want "at least once", so we acknowledge manually after the work.
- `cancelOnError(t -> false)` keeps the subscription alive when an error occurs. The default behaviour cancels the subscription for most errors, after which that consumer silently stops reading, a classic production surprise. The `errorHandler` is where you log or count the error.
- The consumer name must be stable and unique per instance (host name, pod name). Two instances using the same name share a PEL and confuse each other; a name that changes at every restart leaves pending entries behind under dead names.
- The container's `start` and `stop` methods are wired as bean init and destroy methods in the example, so the polling thread follows the application lifecycle.

### Object records

You can avoid manual maps. `ObjectRecord` carries a Java object that is converted through a `HashMapper`; read it with a target type. The reference documentation shows `StreamRecords.newRecord().in("my-stream").ofObject(value)` for writing and `opsForStream().read(User.class, StreamOffset.fromStart("my-stream"))` for reading, and a custom mapper such as the `JacksonHashMapper` (Jackson 3) can be passed to `opsForStream(...)`. For events that several services share, plain string maps with explicit field names are easier to evolve and to inspect with `XRANGE`.

### Failure handling: pending entries, retry, dead letters

Two things go wrong in production. A consumer crashes after reading but before acknowledging, leaving entries in the PEL. Or an entry fails repeatedly (a poisoned message) and would be retried forever. Redis does not redeliver pending entries by itself; your code must look at the PEL and claim entries that have been idle for too long.

blocks.title: PendingReclaimer.java

blocks.text: For this to run, add `@EnableScheduling` to any configuration class. What the reclaimer does: it lists the first 100 pending entries (`XPENDING` with a range), skips those idle for less than a minute, claims the rest for itself (`XCLAIM`, which also bumps the delivery counter) and either processes them or, after five deliveries, copies them to a dead-letter stream and acknowledges the original so that it stops cycling. A real implementation would also persist why the entry failed, and an alert should fire when the DLQ grows.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Idempotent consumers make everything above safe. At-least-once delivery means that after a crash the same order event can be handled twice. Make the handler idempotent: check or set a key such as `idem:email:{orderId}` with `SET` `... NX` before sending, or make the effect naturally repeatable. Redis 8.6 introduces idempotent production (`IDMPAUTO`/`IDMP` arguments to `XADD`) to protect against duplicate producers; the consumer side still needs its own protection.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: The container and many consumers share a connection setup. Each registered subscription issues blocking reads (`XREADGROUP ... BLOCK`). With Lettuce, blocking reads use a dedicated connection rather than the shared one, so a container does not block your other commands, but size your Redis `maxclients` and connection limits knowing that every container adds connections. Do not run the reclaimer and heavy work on the container's executor; give the container its own `executor(...)` in the options if you process slowly.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you get at-least-once processing with Redis Streams in Spring? Create a consumer group, read with `StreamMessageListenerContainer` and manual acknowledgement (`autoAcknowledge(false)`), acknowledge only after the work succeeded, keep the subscription alive on errors, and run a reclaimer that uses `XPENDING` and `XCLAIM` (or `XAUTOCLAIM`) to recover entries abandoned by crashed consumers, with a delivery limit and a dead-letter stream. Make handlers idempotent because duplicates are possible.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- `opsForStream().add` appends, `trim(..., true)` bounds the stream approximately; decide on retention from the start.
- Create the group before consuming and make the consumer name stable and unique per instance.
- Acknowledge manually after success; `receiveAutoAck` gives at-most-once.
- Set `cancelOnError(t -> false)` and an `errorHandler`, otherwise a consumer can stop silently.
- Redis never redelivers pending entries on its own: reclaim idle ones, count deliveries, route poison messages to a dead-letter stream.

Lettuce, the default client, is reactive at its core, and Spring Data Redis exposes that through reactive templates. If your service is built on Spring WebFlux (or you simply want non-blocking composition), you use `ReactiveRedisTemplate` instead of `RedisTemplate`: every method returns a `Mono` or `Flux` and nothing happens until someone subscribes. The commands themselves are the same; only the way you wait for the result changes.

Reactive does not make Redis faster, and a single Lettuce connection already multiplexes concurrent commands in the blocking world too. It pays off when your whole request path is non-blocking, so that a thread is never parked waiting for Redis. Mixing a reactive template into a blocking servlet application mostly adds complexity.

### Dependency and auto-configuration

Use the reactive starter. It brings Lettuce and Reactor, and Boot auto-configures `ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory`, `ReactiveStringRedisTemplate` and a `ReactiveRedisTemplate<Object,Object>`.

  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>
