blocks.text:
### ReactiveStringRedisTemplate in practice

The reactive operations mirror the blocking ones: `opsForValue()`, `opsForHash()`, `opsForList()`, `opsForZSet()` and so on.

blocks.title: VisitCounter.java

blocks.text: What to notice: `increment` returns `Mono<Long>`; the TTL is set only on the first hit. The two commands are not atomic as a pair (a crash between them leaves a key without TTL), which is why production counters use a Lua script or `SET ...` `EX` patterns, as the Patterns part shows. The point here is the shape of the code: you compose steps with `flatMap` and `thenReturn`, never with `.block()`.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Calling .block() inside a reactive chain. `block()` on a Netty event loop thread throws or stalls the loop, and in tests it hides the fact that nothing subscribed. Return the `Mono` to the framework (a WebFlux handler may return it) and let it subscribe.

### A typed reactive template

For objects, define a `ReactiveRedisTemplate` with an explicit serialization context. Unlike the auto-configured generic one, it has the serializers you choose.

blocks.title: ReactiveRedisConfig.java
ReactiveProductCache.java

blocks.text:
The key line is `switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer(...))`: a cache miss is an empty `Mono`, and `Mono.defer` makes sure the loader is only called then (without it, the loader would be called eagerly every time the chain is assembled). A Redis error propagates as an error signal; add `onErrorResume` to fall back to the loader when Redis is unavailable.

### Reactive caching, scripts and streams

- **Spring Cache** annotations can be used on methods that return `Mono` or `Flux`. The abstraction caches the emitted value and not the publisher, and requires a cache implementation with asynchronous retrieval; `RedisCache` has it. Test your actual cache behaviour in an integration test before trusting it.
- **Scripts**: `ReactiveRedisTemplate.execute(script, keys, args)` returns a `Flux` of results, as in the transactions and scripts chapter later in this Part.
- **Pub/Sub**: `ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer` has `receive(ChannelTopic.of("my-channel"))`, which returns a `Flux<ChannelMessage<String, String>>`. It uses the driver threads and needs no executor of its own. `receiveLater` returns a `Mono` that completes once the subscription is confirmed, which is handy to avoid a race between subscribing and publishing in tests.
- **Streams**: `StreamReceiver` (created with `StreamReceiver.create(factory, options)`) returns a `Flux` of records from `receive(StreamOffset.fromStart("stream"))`. It is demand-driven: when the downstream has no demand, polling pauses, and depending on the `ReadOffset` strategy this can cause entries to be skipped. For consumer groups, use the overload that takes a `Consumer` and `StreamOffset` and acknowledge explicitly through `ReactiveStreamOperations.acknowledge`.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Low-level reactive access. Under the templates sits `ReactiveRedisConnection`, with command groups such as `stringCommands()` or `keyCommands()` that work on `ByteBuffer`. You rarely need it; use it for commands that the template does not expose.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- `ReactiveRedisTemplate` and `ReactiveStringRedisTemplate` return `Mono`/`Flux`; nothing runs until subscribed.
- Use the reactive starter and keep the whole request path non-blocking; never `block()` inside a chain.
- Define a typed `ReactiveRedisTemplate` with a `RedisSerializationContext` for objects.
- A cache miss is an empty `Mono`: use `switchIfEmpty(Mono.defer(...))` for cache-aside.
- Reactive streams are demand-driven; read the backpressure notes before using `StreamReceiver` with groups.

HTTP sessions are the classic reason to put Redis into a web application. By default a servlet container keeps each session in the memory of one server. With two instances behind a load balancer you either pin users to an instance ("sticky sessions") and lose their session when that instance restarts, or you move the session out of the instance. Spring Session replaces the container's `HttpSession` implementation with one that stores the session in an external store; Redis is the most common choice because sessions are small, hot, and naturally expire.

### Setting it up in Spring Boot

Add the starter. Boot then auto-configures the session repository for a servlet application (and, in a reactive application, the reactive web session).

blocks.code:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-session-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
blocks.title: pom.xml (dependencies only)

blocks.code:
spring:
  session:
    timeout: 30m
    redis:
      namespace: "shopstream:session"
      flush-mode: on-save
  data:
    redis:
      host: localhost
      port: 6379
server:
  servlet:
    session:
      cookie:
        http-only: true
        secure: true
        same-site: lax
blocks.title: application.yml

blocks.text:
The Boot reference documentation states that the timeout is set with `spring.session.timeout`, and that when it is not set a servlet application falls back to `server.servlet.session.timeout`. The Spring Session Boot guide lists `spring.session.redis.namespace` and `spring.session.redis.flush-mode`. Property names under the session prefix have moved between Boot generations, so open the Common Application Properties appendix for your exact Boot version and search for `spring.session` before you deploy. The behaviour described below does not depend on the names.

If you prefer explicit configuration, the annotation `@EnableRedisHttpSession` (or `@EnableRedisIndexedHttpSession`) switches the auto-configuration off and gives you the same settings as attributes. The Boot guide notes that auto-configuration is equivalent to adding the annotation by hand.

### What lives in Redis

Each session is stored as a Redis hash under a key made from the namespace and the session ID. A typical session, seen from `redis-cli`, looks like this.

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> KEYS spring:session:*
1) "spring:session:sessions:7c9f1e22-1d1b-4c1b-8a39-93b0c9f0a1de"
2) "spring:session:sessions:expires:7c9f1e22-1d1b-4c1b-8a39-93b0c9f0a1de"
3) "spring:session:expirations:1760001600000"
127.0.0.1:6379> HKEYS spring:session:sessions:7c9f1e22-1d1b-4c1b-8a39-93b0c9f0a1de
1) "creationTime"
2) "lastAccessedTime"
3) "maxInactiveInterval"
4) "sessionAttr:cartId"
127.0.0.1:6379> TTL spring:session:sessions:7c9f1e22-1d1b-4c1b-8a39-93b0c9f0a1de
(integer) 2112
blocks.title: Inspect a stored session

blocks.text:
(`KEYS` is used here only on an empty demo instance; on a real one use `SCAN`.) The exact set of keys depends on the repository flavour: the indexed repository additionally maintains the `expires` and `expirations` keys so that it can publish session-expired events, and the simpler repository only uses the session hash with a TTL. Attributes are stored with the prefix `sessionAttr:`. The session cookie in the browser (named `SESSION` by default) carries an encoded session ID, never the data.

### Serialization

By default session attributes are written with Java serialization, so everything you put into a session must be `Serializable`. That works, but it is opaque and fragile across deployments. You can switch to JSON by defining a bean named `springSessionDefaultRedisSerializer` of type `RedisSerializer<Object>`. Be careful: Spring Security stores objects such as the `SecurityContext` in the session, and a JSON serializer must be able to round-trip them, which usually requires registering Spring Security's Jackson modules. If you do not need it, keep the default and keep session attributes small (an ID, not a whole cart).

### Session fixation and cookie safety

**Session fixation** is an attack where an attacker obtains a valid session ID, makes the victim use it (for instance by planting it in a link or cookie), and then waits for the victim to log in; now the attacker's known ID is an authenticated session. The standard defence is to issue a **new session ID on authentication**. Spring Security does this by default (its session-fixation protection changes the session ID on login while keeping the attributes), and Spring Session supports it, because the repository can rotate IDs. Do not turn that protection off.

Also set the cookie flags shown in the YAML: `http-only` hides the cookie from scripts, `secure` sends it only over HTTPS, and `same-site` reduces cross-site request risk. Never put the session ID in a URL.

### Operational notes

- **Memory**: sessions are many small hashes. Measure one with `MEMORY USAGE` and multiply by your peak concurrent sessions before sizing Redis.
- **Expiry**: the TTL on the session key is the idle timeout and is extended on each request. The `flush-mode` decides whether changes are written at once or when the request ends (`on-save`, the default). Attributes you change after the response was committed may not be saved.
- **Persistence and failover**: if Redis loses its data, all users are logged out. With asynchronous replication, a failover can also lose the last writes. For many shops this is acceptable; for others enable AOF or accept re-login.
- **Keyspace notifications**: the indexed repository relies on Redis keyspace events. Spring Session tries to configure `notify-keyspace-events` itself, which fails on managed services that block `CONFIG`. In that case configure the setting in the service console and tell Spring Session not to try (the `ConfigureRedisAction.NO_OP` bean).
- **Redis down means no login**: decide what the application does when it cannot reach the session store, and test it.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Sticky sessions versus a shared session store. Teams often start with sticky sessions, then hit rolling deployments that log everyone out, or autoscaling that unbalances load. A shared store makes instances interchangeable, at the price of one extra Redis round trip per request (typically well under a millisecond on the same network) and a new dependency to monitor.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Spring Session moves the `HttpSession` into Redis; with Boot you add `spring-boot-starter-session-data-redis`.
- Set the idle timeout with `spring.session.timeout`; confirm namespace and flush-mode property names for your Boot version.
- Sessions are hashes with a TTL; attributes use Java serialization unless you provide a serializer bean.
- Keep the session ID rotation on login (session fixation protection) and set `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite` on the cookie.
- Plan for Redis loss: it means logging users out, so decide if that is acceptable.

sections.title: Transactions, Scripts and Pipelines in Spring

blocks.text: Three features let you send several commands as a unit: `MULTI`/`EXEC` transactions, Lua scripts, and pipelining. They solve different problems, and Spring's template API has a different entry point for each. The engine-level semantics (what `EXEC` guarantees, how `WATCH` works, the script cache) are in the Redis Inside part; this chapter is about calling them correctly from Java.

rows: Several commands applied together, no interleaving
Fewer network round trips for independent commands
blocks.caption: Which tool for which need.

blocks.text:
### Why the template needs a SessionCallback

A Redis transaction is bound to one connection: `MULTI`, the queued commands and `EXEC` must all travel over the same connection. Template methods such as `opsForValue().set(...)` normally borrow a connection, run one command and release it, so a `multi()` followed by separate template calls may land on different connections. A `SessionCallback` solves this: it tells the template to use the same connection for everything inside the callback.

blocks.title: StockReservation.java

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- The read happens **before** `multi()`. Inside `MULTI` commands are only queued, so a `get` there would return `null` instead of the value.
- If another client modifies the watched key between `watch` and `exec`, `EXEC` aborts and the template returns an empty or `null` result. The caller must retry or give up. Under contention this loop becomes a retry storm, which is exactly the case for a Lua script instead.
- Redis has no rollback. If a queued command fails at runtime, the others still run. `EXEC` makes the group atomic with respect to other clients, not "all or nothing".

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not call multi() on a template outside a SessionCallback. A bare `redisTemplate.multi()` followed by other template calls is a bug waiting to happen: the commands may use another connection, or the connection may be returned to the pool with an open transaction. The same applies to the `@Transactional` route below.

### @Transactional and transaction support

`RedisTemplate` does not take part in Spring-managed transactions unless you enable it explicitly with `setEnableTransactionSupport(true)` on that template. The reference documentation describes the effect: the connection is bound to the current thread, commands inside the transaction are queued, and when the Spring transaction completes without error the Redis transaction is committed with `EXEC`, otherwise discarded.

There is a catch that surprises people: with transaction support on, **reads inside the transaction return** `null` (they are queued), and the template uses a bound connection that is not returned until the transaction ends. Use it for write-only groups that should follow a database transaction, not for read-modify-write logic. A common alternative is to write to Redis after the database commit with `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)`, which avoids binding Redis to the database transaction at all.

### Lua scripts with RedisScript

For "check something, then change something" with no gap, a Lua script is the right tool. It runs on the server in one step, so no other command can interleave. This is the flash-sale decrement for ShopStream.

blocks.code:
-- KEYS[1] = stock:{sku}   ARGV[1] = quantity wanted
local stock = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]))
if stock == nil then
  return -1
end
local want = tonumber(ARGV[1])
if stock < want then
  return 0
end
redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], want)
return 1
blocks.title: scripts/reserve_stock.lua
InventoryScripts.java

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- Keys go in the `keys` list and other values in the arguments. This is not style: in Redis Cluster the keys declared by a script decide which node runs it, and all keys must be in the same hash slot.
- The script bean is a singleton. The reference documentation recommends a single `DefaultRedisScript` instance so that the SHA1 of the script is not recomputed on each call. The default executor first tries `EVALSHA` and falls back to `EVAL` when the script is not yet in the server's script cache, so you get the saving of not re-sending the script text without managing it.
- The result type must be one of `Long`, `Boolean`, `List`, or a deserialized value type. A Lua `nil` or `false` maps to Java `null` or `false`; a script returning the status `OK` can use no result type.
- Beware of long scripts. A script blocks the whole server while it runs. Keep them to a few commands and never loop over big collections.

### Pipelining

When you have many independent commands, `executePipelined` sends them without waiting for each reply and returns all results at the end. It is the same idea as `redis-benchmark -P` from the labs.

blocks.title: CartCountLoader.java

blocks.text: The callback must return `null`; the template collects the replies. The template deserializes the results with the serializers you configured, as the reference documentation notes. A pipeline is **not** atomic: other clients' commands can interleave, and one failing command does not stop the rest. A pipeline also holds all replies in memory, so batch very large jobs (for example 500 to 1000 commands at a time).

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Pipelines and transactions on a shared connection. Do not mix a bound transaction and `executePipelined` casually. With transaction support enabled, the results of a pipeline inside a transaction come back only when the transaction completes, and your code sees surprising values. Keep the two features in separate code paths.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Use a `SessionCallback` so that `WATCH`, `MULTI` and `EXEC` share one connection; read before `multi()`.
- `RedisTemplate` joins `@Transactional` only after `setEnableTransactionSupport(true)`, and reads inside return `null`.
- Use a Lua `RedisScript` for atomic read-decide-write; pass keys as keys, keep one script bean, keep scripts short.
- `executePipelined` cuts round trips but is not atomic.

Code that talks to Redis needs two kinds of tests. Unit tests check your logic with Redis out of the picture. Integration tests check that your keys, serializers, TTLs and scripts really work against a real Redis server, because the interesting bugs live exactly there: wrong key names, a serializer that cannot read what it wrote, a Lua script with a typo.

### Unit tests: keep Redis away

For a service that only uses a template in a few places, mock the template. The code under test does not know whether it talks to Redis or to a fake.

blocks.title: ProductEventPublisherTest.java

blocks.text:
This is cheap and fast, but it proves nothing about Redis. Keep such tests for branching logic and use real Redis for everything else.

### Integration tests with Testcontainers

Testcontainers starts a real Redis in Docker for the test run. It needs a Docker daemon on the machine (and in CI). Spring Boot connects it to your application with `@ServiceConnection`: the container's host and mapped port replace `spring.data.redis.*` for the test context, so you configure nothing by hand.

blocks.code:
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-testcontainers</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
  <artifactId>testcontainers</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
blocks.title: pom.xml (test dependencies)
RedisTestConfig.java

blocks.text:
The `name = "redis"` attribute is required: Spring Boot cannot tell from a `GenericContainer` which image it runs, so the name is the hint that selects the Redis connection details. Because the container is a Spring bean, Spring starts it before the beans that need it and stops it when the context closes; you do not need the JUnit `@Testcontainers` extension.

Now a real test of the stock script and the cache, using the full application context.

blocks.title: InventoryIT.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: every test starts from an empty database, because leftovers from one test make the next one flaky; flushing is acceptable here because this Redis exists only for the test run. Never run this against a shared instance. The class name ends in `IT` by convention so that a build tool can run it in the integration phase.

If you cannot use `@ServiceConnection`, the older approach works on every version: start the container in a static field and publish its address with a `@DynamicPropertySource` method that calls `registry.add("spring.data.redis.host",` `...)` and `registry.add("spring.data.redis.port", ...)`.

### Test slices

Boot 4 has a Redis test slice, `@DataRedisTest`, in the module `spring-boot-data-redis-test` (package `org.springframework.boot.data.redis.test.autoconfigure`). It starts only the Redis auto-configuration (connection factory, templates, repositories) and not your whole application, so it is faster for tests that only exercise Redis code. The slice does not component-scan your services, so import what you need.

blocks.title: ProductEventPublisherSliceTest.java

blocks.text:
The slice list in the Boot reference shows that this slice imports the Redis, reactive Redis and Redis repository auto-configurations plus SSL and the optional Testcontainers service-connection auto-configuration. The name of the matching starter artifact for test scope is not something this book could confirm; the module `spring-boot-data-redis-test` is the one that holds the annotation.

### Embedded Redis and fakes

Several community libraries start an "embedded" Redis binary inside the test JVM, and there are in-memory fakes that speak the Redis protocol. They look convenient, but they have three problems: they usually lag behind current Redis versions, they implement only part of the commands (rarely Lua details, Streams edge cases, or module commands such as JSON), and they behave differently from the real server in exactly the places you want to test. A container with the same image tag as production avoids all three. Use a fake only if Docker is truly unavailable, and then limit its use to trivial key-value tests.

### Making tests reliable

- **Pin the image tag** to the major version you run, for example `redis:8`, so tests change only when you change them.
- **Reuse the container** across test classes: a static or shared configuration starts it once per test run. Starting a container per test method is slow.
- **Test expiry without sleeping**: set a short TTL in the test configuration, or assert on `redis.getExpire(key)`, instead of `Thread.sleep`. For logic that depends on time, inject a `Clock`.
- **Test Redis being down**: stop the container (or point the test at a closed port) and assert that your `CacheErrorHandler` and timeouts keep the service answering.
- **Assert on the keys**: a test that scans for `product:*` and expects exactly one key catches key-name regressions that mocks cannot see.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Unit tests mock the template for logic; integration tests use a real Redis from Testcontainers (`redis:8`).
- `@Bean @ServiceConnection(name = "redis") GenericContainer<?>` wires the container to the application; the `name` is required for `GenericContainer`.
- `@DataRedisTest` is the Redis test slice in Boot 4; `@DynamicPropertySource` is the manual alternative.
- Clean the database before each test and avoid sleeping; test failure paths too.
- Prefer a real container over embedded or fake Redis.

A Redis-backed Spring service has two places to look when something is wrong: Redis itself (its `INFO` output, slow log, memory; see the Operations part) and the application's view of Redis: how long commands take from the client side, how many connections are open, whether the cache is doing its job. This chapter covers the application side.

### Health

With Spring Boot Actuator on the classpath and a Redis connection factory present, a Redis health indicator is registered automatically and appears as the `redis` component of `/actuator/health`. It reports `UP` when it can talk to Redis and includes the server version in the details. Show details only to authorised users:

blocks.code:
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,metrics,prometheus
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized
      probes:
        enabled: true
blocks.title: application.yml

blocks.text:
Think before tying Redis health to your Kubernetes **readiness** or **liveness** probe. If Redis is only a cache and the service can serve from the database, a Redis outage should not take every pod out of rotation (that turns a performance problem into a full outage). If Redis is a hard dependency (a session store), a failing readiness probe is correct. Decide per service, and keep liveness independent from Redis in either case.

### Metrics

Three groups of metrics matter.

#### Cache hit ratio

When statistics are enabled on the cache manager (`enableStatistics()` or `spring.cache.redis.enable-statistics:` `true`), Micrometer's cache instrumentation binds the caches, and you get meters such as `cache.gets` with a `result` tag of `hit` or `miss`, and `cache.puts`. The hit ratio is hits divided by all gets. Graph it per cache. A cache below, say, 50% for a read-heavy path deserves a look at its TTL, key design or whether it should exist at all. Treat that number as a prompt for investigation, not as a universal target.

#### Client-side command latency

Lettuce can record command latency through Micrometer. Register your own `ClientResources` bean with a Micrometer recorder; Boot's auto-configured resources step aside when you define one.

blocks.title: LettuceMetricsConfig.java

blocks.text:
The recorder publishes timers with a `lettuce` prefix, tagged by command and host. This is the number that tells you what your application experiences, including network and queueing, which the server-side `SLOWLOG` cannot show. Compare the two when users complain about latency but the slow log is empty. Check the Lettuce reference for the exact meter names of your version before building dashboards on them.

#### Connections and pool

If you use pooling (`commons-pool2` on the classpath), track active and idle connections with the pool's own metrics or JMX. On the server, watch `connected_clients` in `INFO clients`. A client count that rises with traffic and never falls is a leak or a missing pool limit.

### Logging

Keep `io.lettuce.core` and `org.springframework.data.redis` at `INFO` or `WARN` in production. Raise `io.lettuce.core` to `DEBUG` temporarily to see connection and reconnect events when you are chasing a flaky network. Do not enable `TRACE`: it logs every command and can leak data into the logs. Log cache errors from your `CacheErrorHandler` at `WARN` with the cache name and key (never the value), and count them with a metric so that a silent Redis outage shows on a dashboard.

### Production checklist

rows: `spring.data.redis.timeout` (command timeout) and `connect-timeout` are set to values you chose, not left at defaults; the service fails fast when Redis is slow
One shared Lettuce connection is usually enough; pooling is configured deliberately if you use blocking calls or transactions
Redis ACL user with only the commands and key patterns needed; TLS enabled (`spring.data.redis.ssl.bundle`); password in a secret store
A prefix per service or environment; no `KEYS` calls; explicit cache keys
Every cache has a TTL; session and idempotency keys have TTLs; jitter on mass-loaded caches
JSON serializers chosen on purpose; no Java serialization in shared data; a plan for schema changes
`CacheErrorHandler` in place; behaviour with Redis down tested; circuit breaker or fallback where the user path depends on Redis
`maxmemory` and `maxmemory-policy` set on the server; no unbounded streams, lists or sets
Group created at startup; manual ack; reclaimer and dead-letter stream; trimming policy
Health indicator, hit ratio, Lettuce latency, connection count, error counters on a dashboard with alerts
Testcontainers integration tests with the same Redis major version as production
Rolling restarts handled: stable consumer names, graceful container shutdown, reconnect behaviour tested with a failover
blocks.caption: Spring and Redis, before go-live.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: The first outage is rarely Redis being down. Typical first incidents in Spring services: a cache without TTL that fills memory until the eviction policy (or `noeviction` errors) bites; a missing timeout so that threads pile up behind a slow Redis; a stream consumer that stopped after the first exception; a `KEYS` call in an admin endpoint. Every item in the checklist above exists because teams have hit it.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How would you monitor a Spring Boot service that uses Redis as a cache? From the application: the cache hit ratio per cache (Micrometer, statistics enabled), Lettuce command latency, error counts from the cache error handler, and the health indicator. From Redis: memory use against `maxmemory`, evicted and expired keys, connected clients, slow log and latency. Alert on a falling hit ratio, rising latency percentiles, evictions when you did not expect them, and rising error counts.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- The Redis health indicator is automatic with Actuator; think carefully before wiring it into readiness probes.
- Enable cache statistics for hit ratio; register a Micrometer command latency recorder for Lettuce.
- Log cache errors without values, keep `TRACE` off in production, and count failures.
- Walk the checklist: timeouts, ACL and TLS, TTLs on everything, failure behaviour, bounded memory, tested stream consumers.
